composing_text: CAN-INF-002D (under command from 15:00 on 11 July); CAN-INF-003D (under command from 15:00 on 11 July)
current_activity: Takes over about 8000 yards of the Caen front at 15:00 with the 2nd and 3rd Divisions
notes: Event date: 11 July 1944, 15:00 (Stacey, p. 166). Event definition: II Canadian Corps (Stacey: 2nd Canadian Corps) becomes operational and takes over about 8000 yards of front in the Caen sector, with the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Infantry Divisions, the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and the 2nd Canadian Army Group Royal Artillery under command; it is under Second Army (inferred from pp. 146 and 200). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 166: "General Simonds' 2nd Canadian Corps had now entered the line"; "At 3:00 p.m. on 11 July it took over about 8000 yards of front in the Caen sector; with the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Infantry Divisions, the 2nd Canadian Armoured Brigade and the 2nd Canadian 60 Army Group Royal Artillery under command"; p. 146: "He had told General Dempsey to place the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division under the 2nd Canadian Corps as soon as the latter could take over operational responsibility". Location: Caen sector (existing area place PL0059) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place for the Caen sector and stands for the corps front; no corps headquarters position is given on these pages (Main Headquarters was at Camilly from early July, p. 152). Location support: Stacey names the Caen sector and an 8000-yard front, with no town or coordinates. Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

current_activity: Opens Operation Atlantic: 3rd Division attacks Colombelles, Giberville and Mondeville east of the Orne
notes: Event date: 18 July 1944 (Stacey, p. 171). Event definition: Operation Atlantic opens on 18 July, with the 3rd Division advancing from the Orne bridgehead through Colombelles and Vaucelles and the 2nd Division to follow south of Caen; Stacey dates the operations east of the Orne 18-21 July (p. 176). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 171: "The 8th Brigade was to lead the advance east of the river, capturing Colombelles, Giberville and Mondeville"; p. 176: "the operations of 18-21 July east of the Orne". Location: Colombelles, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Colombelles as the first objective of the corps attack (p. 171). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

composing_text: UK-ARM-007D (under the corps since 20 July); UK-ARM-GRDD (under the corps since 20 July); CAN-INF-002D (first phase); CAN-INF-003D (first phase)
current_activity: Opens Operation Spring at 03:30: 2nd and 3rd Divisions attack Verrieres Ridge and Tilly-la-Campagne
notes: Event date: 25 July 1944, 03:30 (Stacey, p. 186). Event definition: Operation Spring: the corps attacks south of Caen to capture the line May-sur-Orne, Verrieres and Tilly-la-Campagne in the first phase; the 7th Armoured and Guards Armoured Divisions are under the corps from 20 July (p. 186). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 186: "D Day was confirmed as 25 July and H Hour as 3:30 a.m."; "These two latter divisions had been under the 2nd Canadian Corps since 20 July". Location: Verrieres Ridge, Calvados with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Verrieres as an objective of the first phase (p. 186). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

current_activity: Passes from Second Army to First Canadian Army at noon with the front south of Caen
notes: Event date: 31 July 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 201). Event definition: II Canadian Corps (Stacey: 2nd Canadian Corps) passes from Second Army to First Canadian Army at noon, together with the front south of Caen; 4th Armoured Division joins the corps in the line the same day. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 201: "to take under its command General Simonds' 2nd Canadian Corps and with it the front south of Caen"; "finally happened at noon on 31 July"; p. 200: "under which at this moment the 2nd Canadian Corps was still serving". Location: Caen sector (existing area place PL0059) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place and stands for the corps front. Location support: Stacey names the front south of Caen, no town. Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

composing_text: CAN-INF-002D (assault division); CAN-INF-003D (assault division); CAN-ARM-004D (armoured division in the second phase); UK-INF-051D (from midnight 3-4 August; reverted at 13:00 on 9 August); POL-ARM-001D (from 06:00 on 5 August)
current_activity: Opens Operation Totalize at 23:30: night attack down the Caen-Falaise road
notes: Event date: 7 August 1944, 23:30 (Stacey, pp. 218-219). Event definition: Operation Totalize: after the Bomber Command attack from 23:00 the armoured columns and marching infantry cross the start line at 23:30 on the night of 7-8 August, south of Caen astride the Falaise road. The 51st (Highland) Division is under the corps from midnight 3-4 August until 13:00 on 9 August and the 1st Polish Armoured Division from 06:00 on 5 August. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 219: "At 11:30 the armoured columns and the marching infantry moved forward into the darkness"; p. 218: "Bomber Command was to begin its attack at 11:00 p.m."; p. 208: "At midnight of 3-4 August the 51st (Highland) Infantry Division and the 33rd British Armoured Brigade passed to its command from the 1st British Corps"; "under General Simonds at 6:00 a.m. on 5 August"; p. 229: "At 1:00 p.m. the 51st reverted to the command of the 1st British Corps". Location: Caen sector (existing area place PL0059) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the existing area place and stands for the start line; the exact start line is a line, not a point. Location support: Stacey names the start line astride the Caen-Falaise road south of Caen; the 2nd Division columns formed up south of Ifs (p. 216). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

current_activity: Opens Operation Tractable by day: 3rd and 4th Divisions cross the Laison valley
notes: Event date: 14 August 1944, about 11:42 (Stacey, pp. 240-241). Event definition: Operation Tractable: the armoured columns of the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division (right) and the 4th Canadian Armoured Division (left) cross a start line north of Estrees-la-Campagne behind smoke and Bomber Command, and cross the Laison valley, a reserve squadron of the 1st Hussars finding a crossing at Rouvres. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history); the operation row for Tractable is not added, the claim uses the existing Falaise battle row. Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 240: "the start-line, to be crossed at H Hour, was a line running slightly north of Estrees-la-Campagne and through Soignolles"; p. 241: "On the 3rd Division front on the right most of the tanks of two squadrons of the 1st Hussars suffered the former fate; the reserve squadron discovered a crossing at Rouvres"; "Late in the afternoon the armoured advance on this front was proceeding beyond the Laison". Location: Rouvres, Calvados with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the Laison crossings (Rouvres, Maizieres, Ernes) lie along a line a few miles long; the point is one of them. Location support: Stacey names Rouvres as the crossing found on the right of the Laison on the first day (p. 241). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

current_activity: The Falaise Gap is finally and completely closed after contact with the Poles
notes: Event date: 21 August 1944 (Stacey, p. 264). Event definition: After contact across the Gap was first made at Chambois on the evening of 19 August (p. 261) and the German break-out of 20 August, the Gap is finally and completely closed on 21 August; the corps commander had conferred with his four divisional commanders on 19 August. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 264: "As a result of the day's operations firm contact was made with the Poles and the Gap finally and completely closed"; p. 259: "At 11:00 a.m. on 19 August Simonds again conferred with his four divisional commanders". Location: Saint-Lambert-sur-Dives and Chambois (midpoint, existing place PL0514) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the midpoint between the two villages and stands for the closing line. Location support: Stacey places the fighting at St. Lambert, Trun and Chambois (pp. 259-264). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

current_activity: First Seine crossing: a platoon crosses near Criquebeuf at 17:00; corps assaults at Pont de l Arche and Elbeuf
notes: Event date: 26 August 1944, 17:00 (Stacey, p. 283). Event definition: The first Canadians cross the Seine, a scout platoon and a company of the Lincoln and Welland Regiment near Criquebeuf above Elbeuf; the corps plan has the 4th Division take a bridgehead at Pont de l Arche and Criquebeuf and the 3rd Division one at Elbeuf (p. 287). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 283: "crossed the Seine near Criquebeuf, above Elbeuf"; p. 282: "The 2nd Canadian Corps was to plan and make initial preparations for an opposed crossing of the Seine between Pont de l'Arche and Elbeuf"; p. 287: "The 3rd Division would seize in the same manner a bridgehead including Elbeuf and the railway bridge at Port du Gravier to the north". Location: Criquebeuf-sur-Seine, Eure with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Stacey names Criquebeuf as the place of the first crossing (p. 283). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

composing_text: POL-ARM-001D (passes under the 1st British Corps on 28 September)
current_activity: Front reduced: 2nd Division placed temporarily under I Corps; the Polish division follows on 28 September
notes: Event date: 26 September 1944 (Stacey, p. 367). Event definition: Simonds had told the Army commander on 22 September that a corps headquarters could not control four divisions from Boulogne to east of Antwerp; on 26 September the 2nd Canadian Division goes temporarily under I Corps and on 28 September the 1st Polish Armoured Division also passes under General Crocker. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 367: "On the 26th the 2nd Canadian Corps' front was reduced by placing the 2nd Canadian Division temporarily under the 1st British Corps"; "On the 28th the 1st Polish Armoured Division, having moved to the area south-east of Antwerp, also passed under General Crocker's command"; "it was difficult for a corps headquarters to control four divisions operating on diverse tasks from Boulogne to east of Antwerp". Location: Antwerp, Belgium with a precision of 50 km. Location approximate: the point is a representative one for the corps area, not a headquarters position. Location support: Stacey gives the corps front only as the line from Boulogne to east of Antwerp (p. 367) and no corps headquarters place. Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).

composing_text: CAN-INF-002D (right of the corps front, between Cuijk and Groesbeek)
current_activity: Takes over the Nijmegen sector from 30th Corps; control passes to First Canadian Army at noon
notes: Event date: 9 November 1944, noon (Stacey, p. 428). Event definition: II Canadian Corps takes over the Nijmegen bridgehead from the British 30th Corps, which passes to Second Army; the front runs from Cuijk past Groesbeek and Nijmegen to the island beyond the Waal, held by the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Divisions and the 50th and 101st Airborne Divisions (pp. 428 and 430); Simonds returns to the corps from commanding the Army. Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 428: "Control of the Nijmegen bridgehead actually passed to First Canadian Army at noon on 9 November"; "The 2nd Canadian Corps was directed to take over the Nijmegen sector from the 30th British Corps"; p. 430: "The 2nd Canadian Corps had assumed its new responsibilities in the Nijmegen bridgehead with four divisions in the line". Location: Nijmegen, Gelderland with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the city and stands for the corps sector, which runs from Cuijk to the island beyond the Waal. Location support: Stacey names the Nijmegen sector and bridgehead (pp. 428, 430). Commander: Lt.-Gen. G. G. Simonds (Stacey, Appendix G, p. 664: 30 Jan. 44 to 25 Jun. 45).
